lesson.title: Est-ce que Drills
lesson.subtitle: 'Is it that': turn statements into questions without moving a single word.

hook.title: The Zero-Inversion Question Opener
hook.content: est-ce que ('is it that') absorbs the question inversion inside itself, leaving your statement untouched after que! And before a vowel-initial pronoun (il, elle, on), que elides to qu': Est-ce qu'il est là ? Est-ce qu'elle parle français ? Est-ce qu'on y va ?

footnotes.title: Why Est-ce que is the learner's best friend
footnotes.content: With Est-ce que in front, you never have to invert verb and pronoun or worry about word order!

pattern.title: Est-ce que + Consonant Subject; Est-ce qu' + Vowel Subject (il, elle, on)
pattern.content: Snap Est-ce que or Est-ce qu' onto the front of any statement to turn it into a clean question.
pattern.linguist_note: Est-ce que is pronounced /ɛs kə/ before consonants and /ɛs.k‿/ before vowels.
pattern.trap_note: Don't invert the verb when you already used est-ce que (*Est-ce que veux-tu) — keep normal statement order!

exercises.prompt: Match each statement with its est-ce que question:
exercises.target_answer: Est-ce que tu parles français, Est-ce que vous avez l'heure, Est-ce qu'il est ici, Est-ce qu'elle vient ce soir
exercises.meaning: Tu parles français, Vous avez l'heure, Il est ici (vowel subject!), Elle vient ce soir (vowel subject!)
exercises.explanation: que elides to qu' before il, elle, and on.

exercises.prompt: How do you turn 'Il a compris' ('He understood') into an est-ce que question?
exercises.explanation: que elides before vowel-initial il: Est-ce qu'il a compris.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal structure of 'Est-ce que tu parles français'?
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: Is-it that you speak French
exercises.explanation: Est-ce que literally means 'Is-it that', replacing English 'Do'.

exercises.idea: do you have a reservation (polite vous, using Est-ce que)
exercises.target_answer: Est-ce que vous avez une réservation
exercises.explanation: Est-ce que + vous avez une réservation keeps normal word order.

diagnosis.cue: Pair vous with avez after Est-ce que.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Est-ce que tu veux un café
exercises.target_answer: Est-ce que tu veux un café
exercises.explanation: Zero word-order change after Est-ce que.
exercises.affirmation: You built the Est-ce que question cleanly.

summary.outcome: Turn any statement into a question with Est-ce que and elide it to Est-ce qu' before il, elle, on.

use_example.german: Est-ce qu'on va au café maintenant ?
use_example.english: Are we going to the café now?

summary.takeaway: Est-ce que absorbs the inversion so your sentence never has to move.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([702] Question-Word Twins): see how Est-ce que Drills leads directly into Question-Word Twins.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "Do you have a reservation" in French:
twist.target_answer: Est-ce que vous avez une réservation
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Est-ce que vous avez une réservation" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Est-ce que Drills.

est_ce_que.context_phrase: Est-ce que tu veux le gâteau ?
est_ce_que.etymology_derivation: Literally 'is it that you want…' — a question scaffolded out of a statement, no word order changed.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

aller.context_translation: I'm going to go to the café.
aller.etymology_derivation: Latin ambulāre 'to walk' → ambler → aller. To go is a stroll away — and the near future rides on it.

français.etymology_derivation: Not capitalized when naming the language in French.
